succession.name: Shogunal Hereditary
succession.description: The Shōgun's office passes from father to son within the bakufu's ruling house. The Imperial court in Kyōto formally invests each new Shōgun, but the line itself is fixed — Minamoto, then Ashikaga, then Tokugawa — and a clan that loses the office rarely recovers it. Adoption into the line is recognised but the choice rests with the household elders, not the realm at large.

succession.name: Daimyō Elective
succession.description: When a daimyō dies, the clan's senior retainers — its karō — gather to acclaim a successor. The first call goes to the daimyō's chosen heir, but a child too young to lead in war can be passed over for an adopted brother-in-arms, a son-in-law, or even a senior retainer raised into the family name. The succession is therefore hereditary in intent and elective in fact.

succession.name: Ikkō Confederation
succession.description: The Ikkō-Ikki recognise no temporal sovereign but the Monshu, hereditary head of the Honganji line, descendant of Shinran. When the Monshu names a successor the kō — the leagues of farmers, ji-samurai and lay priests — are expected to affirm him. In practice the office descends in the Honganji bloodline; in theory the community can refuse, and at moments of crisis it has.
